name: Biotechnology Ignition Grant (BIG)
provider: BIRAC, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Up to ₹50 lakh grant-in-aid over up to 18 months, released in 3–4 milestone instalments (₹20 lakh on signing, then up to ₹20 lakh per milestone, last ₹5 lakh after the final report).
timeToMoney: Not published as a fixed number. After a call closes there is an eligibility check, online review by 3–5 experts, a face-to-face pitch to BIRAC's Technical Expert Panel, then up to 45 days of due diligence before the first ₹20 lakh is released on signing.
deadline: Last call (BIG-25) closed 30 Nov 2025. Guidelines say calls come at least twice a year (typically 1 January and 1 July) and stay open about 30 days, but no 2026 BIG call was listed on BIRAC's call page as of 27 Oct 2026.
oneLiner: India's best-known first grant for biotech startups: up to ₹50 lakh, no equity, to turn a lab idea into a working proof of concept.
what: BIG is BIRAC's flagship scheme for very early biotech startups. It pays for the research work needed to prove an idea works (proof of concept): manpower, consumables, small equipment, incubator rent, IP filing, outsourcing and travel. It does not pay for basic research, PhD work, or late-stage clinical or field trials. The money is a grant, so you do not give up shares or repay it.
who: A company or LLP registered in India, incorporated not more than 5 years before the date the BIG call opens (Guidelines v9, Oct 2025).
At least 51% owned by resident Indian citizens (directly or through Indian-owned companies).
A named Project Leader who has at least an undergraduate degree, holds shares in the company and will pitch to the selection panel.
Has its own working lab, or is incubated at an incubator (the BIG Partner verifies this).

Proposal falls in one of seven categories: devices & diagnostics; drugs incl. delivery; industrial biotech incl. secondary agriculture; agriculture; biosimilars & stem cells; vaccines; bioinformatics.
notFor: Individuals without a company: the October 2025 guidelines list only a registered company or LLP as eligible.
Anyone who has already received BIG once (support is given only once per startup).
Basic or exploratory research, low-novelty ideas, projects without a real biotech component, and late-stage clinical/field trials.
Companies (or promoters) in default on BIRAC loans, and companies whose 20%+ promoters run another ineligible biotech company/LLP.
Projects whose same objectives have already been funded by another agency.
why: It is non-dilutive: ₹50 lakh with no equity taken, at the stage when investors are least willing to fund you.
A BIG award is a strong signal to biotech angels and to BIRAC's own follow-on schemes (SEED, LEAP, SBIRI, BIPP).
You get a BIG Partner (an experienced bio-incubator) that mentors and monitors you for the full 18 months.
It forces you to set clear technical milestones, which makes the next fundraise easier.
howItWorks: BIRAC runs BIG through a network of BIG Partners (8 partners named on the BIRAC page). You apply online on the BIRAC portal during an open call. The BIG Partner checks eligibility and plagiarism, sends eligible proposals to 3–5 subject experts for online review, and a review committee shortlists teams. Shortlisted teams pitch face-to-face to a Technical Expert Panel run centrally by BIRAC. Selected teams then go through financial, legal and technical due diligence (including a possible site visit) and must accept the offer within about 30–45 days. The BIG Partner signs the grant agreement on BIRAC's behalf, releases ₹20 lakh on signing and the rest against milestones, and monitors progress. Scoring weights: unmet need 20, value proposition 20, technical viability 30, team 15, business perspective 15.

steps.title: Incorporate and set up your lab access
steps.detail: Register a private limited company or LLP (51%+ Indian-owned) and secure lab space, either your own or through an incubator that will give you a letter of intent.

steps.title: Register on the BIRAC portal
steps.detail: Create a user account on birac.nic.in before the call opens and read the BIG Guidelines and proposal proformas linked from the BIG page.

steps.title: Write the proposal during the open call
steps.detail: Calls are open for roughly 30 days. Cover the unmet need, your novelty, preliminary data, an 18-month milestone plan and a budget within ₹50 lakh. Submit online only; changes are not allowed after submission.

steps.title: Clear eligibility check and expert review
steps.detail: The BIG Partner screens for eligibility and scheme fit; 3–5 reviewers score the science; a review committee shortlists.

steps.title: Pitch to the Technical Expert Panel
steps.detail: The Project Leader presents in person to BIRAC's panel. Have undertakings from advisors and key team members and evidence of access to facilities or samples ready.

steps.title: Due diligence and offer acceptance
steps.detail: Within 30–45 days, complete document verification, budget justification with quotations, and finalise milestones with the BIG Partner, or the offer lapses.

steps.title: Sign the grant agreement and receive the first tranche
steps.detail: The BIG Partner signs on behalf of BIRAC and releases ₹20 lakh. Later tranches follow satisfactory milestone reviews; the last ₹5 lakh comes after the final report, utilisation certificate and statement of expenditure.

documents: Certificate of incorporation and shareholding pattern (showing 51%+ Indian ownership)
Project Leader's degree certificate and proof of shareholding
Detailed proposal in BIRAC's BIG proforma, with preliminary data
Letter of interest or MoU from your incubator, or proof of your own lab
Undertakings from scientific advisors/mentors and key technical team members
Evidence of access to any unique facilities or samples the project needs
Quotations backing the budget (asked for during due diligence)
Undertaking that the same objectives have not been funded by another agency
benefits: Up to ₹50 lakh non-dilutive grant
Mentoring from the BIG Partner on technology, IP, legal, regulatory and business questions
Investor connects, trainings and networking through BIRAC's ecosystem
Credibility that helps with SEED/LEAP equity and later SBIRI/BIPP grants
pros: No equity and no repayment.
Large amount for a first grant, enough to hire a small team and run real experiments.
Clear, published scoring criteria and process.
Strong mentoring network through BIG Partners.
cons: You must already have a company; the Oct 2025 guidelines no longer list individuals as eligible.
Calls have become irregular: one in 2024 (BIG-24) and one in Nov 2025 (BIG-25), and none listed in 2026 so far.
Highly competitive: recent final lists carry roughly 49–60 names per call nationwide.
Paperwork-heavy: milestones, utilisation certificates and audits; the last ₹5 lakh is paid only as a reimbursement at the end.
Only one BIG per startup, ever.
goodFitIf: You are a biotech, medtech, diagnostics or agri-bio founder with early lab data showing your idea can work.
Your company is under 5 years old and you have lab access (own or incubator).
You need 12–18 months of runway to reach proof of concept without giving up equity.
skipIf: Your product is pure software with no real biotech component.
You are already past proof of concept and need money for trials or scale-up (look at SBIRI, BIPP or LEAP instead).
You have not yet incorporated and are not ready to.
You have received BIG before.
insiderTips: Pick your incubator early: a letter of intent from an incubator is needed before the expert panel stage, and many winners are incubated at BIG Partners.
Write to the scoring sheet: technical viability carries 30 of 100 marks, so lead with preliminary data and a believable 18-month plan.
Register on the BIRAC portal well before a call; calls are short (about 30 days) and the portal shuts automatically at the deadline.
Keep the budget tight and backed by quotations; BIG Partners check every line during due diligence.

performance.summary: BIG started in July 2012. BIRAC's 2016 report counted 192 projects approved in its first four years; by August 2023 the government told Parliament that around 900 projects had been supported. Recent calls each produced roughly 49–60 awardees according to BIRAC's published final lists (BIG-24's list is marked 'subject to due diligence and budget availability'). Year-wise rupee amounts are not published.

name: Small Business Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI)
provider: BIRAC, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Grant-in-aid with cost sharing. A startup (under 10 years old) that has never had a BIRAC grant gets up to 100% of its budget up to ₹50 lakh, plus up to 70% of anything above ₹50 lakh. Other companies get up to 70% of their budget. No overall cap is published. A 5% royalty on product sales applies until the royalty equals the grant.
equity: None, but 5% royalty on annual net sales of the resulting product until total royalty equals the grant received
duration: Project-specific; money released in about four milestone instalments
timeToMoney: Not published. Proposals go through expert committees and a site visit; the first instalment follows signing of the Grant-in-aid Letter Agreement, a separate royalty agreement and other pre-disbursement formalities.
deadline: Last call ran 1 Apr – 30 May 2025. Guidelines say two calls a year (1 Apr–15 May and 1 Sep–15 Oct), but no SBIRI call was listed on BIRAC's call page after May 2025 as of 27 Oct 2026.
oneLiner: A BIRAC grant for small biotech companies to take an idea with proof of principle to a validated product or process (up to TRL 6).
what: SBIRI is DBT's oldest early-stage public-private partnership scheme for biotech, started in 2005. It funds companies (alone or with an academic partner) doing early, high-risk R&D that already has proof of principle and preliminary data. Projects should end at Technology Readiness Level 6 or below. The support is grant-in-aid, with the company paying part of the cost and a royalty on future sales.
who: A company registered under the Companies Act 2013 or an LLP, alone or in a consortium.
At least 51% of shares held by Indian citizens with Indian passports (OCI/PIO holders do not count); for LLPs, at least half the partners must be Indian citizens.
Adequate in-house R&D facilities (checked on a site visit) or incubation at a recognised incubator.
Optional academic partner: public or private universities, national labs, or registered not-for-profit research bodies.
notFor: Ideas without proof of principle or preliminary data (concept-only or exploratory research is rejected).
Companies, subsidiaries or directors that have defaulted on BIRAC loans, refunds or royalties.
Companies that withdrew an Apex-Committee-approved proposal or had a project foreclosed for irregularities (debarred for the next 2 calls).
Individuals without a registered company or LLP.
why: Larger budgets than BIG, and a startup's first ₹50 lakh can be 100% funded.
No equity taken; you repay only through a capped royalty if the product sells.
You can bring in a university or national lab as a funded partner.
SBIRI has a track record: 337 projects supported and 87 products or technologies developed or commercialised (as of 31 Jan 2024).
howItWorks: BIRAC opens SBIRI calls on its portal. Proposals are reviewed by expert committees on novelty, preliminary data, strength of proof of concept, clarity of strategy and national or social relevance, with a site visit to check facilities. Approved projects sign a Grant-in-aid Letter Agreement and a separate royalty agreement. Funds go to the company (and to the academic partner, if any) in roughly four instalments, each released only after the linked milestone is achieved. The company contributes its share of cost (at least 30% unless it qualifies for the startup 100%-up-to-₹50-lakh rule) and pays 5% of net sales of the resulting product as royalty until the royalty matches the grant.

steps.title: Check your stage
steps.detail: Make sure you have proof of principle and preliminary data, and that the project can reach a defined outcome by TRL 6.

steps.title: Register your company on the BIRAC portal
steps.detail: Create an organisation login on birac.nic.in; proposals can only be filed by registered users during an active call.

steps.title: Line up partners and co-funding
steps.detail: Decide whether an academic partner is needed and confirm how your company will fund its share (30% for non-first-time grantees).

steps.title: Submit the proposal online during the call window
steps.detail: Use the SBIRI proforma, with milestones, budget and preliminary data. Watch for the call notice on BIRAC's Call for Proposals page.

steps.title: Expert review and site visit
steps.detail: Committees score the proposal; BIRAC may inspect your facilities or incubator.

steps.title: Sign agreements and complete pre-disbursement formalities
steps.detail: Sign the Grant-in-aid Letter Agreement and royalty agreement, pass a board resolution, open a no-lien account and submit in-house R&D and shareholding certificates.

steps.title: Receive milestone-linked instalments
steps.detail: The first instalment comes on signing; later ones follow technical milestones and the final project completion report.

Board resolution and letter of authorisation (BIRAC formats)
No-lien bank account letter

Academic partner's registration/accreditation documents (if any)
Audited financials showing ability to fund your share
benefits: Grant funding for high-risk R&D
Optional funded academic collaboration
BIRAC project monitoring and mentoring
Pathway to BIPP for later-stage, larger projects
pros: Startups' first ₹50 lakh can be 100% grant-funded.
No equity dilution.
Lets you fund an academic partner inside the same project.
Long-running scheme with published impact numbers.
cons: 5% royalty on product sales until it equals the grant.
Cost sharing: established companies must fund at least 30%.
No SBIRI call has been listed since May 2025 (as of 27 Oct 2026).
Requires proof of principle; not for pure idea-stage teams.
Heavy documentation and milestone audits.
goodFitIf: You are a biotech company with proof-of-principle data and need to build and validate a prototype.
You want to partner with a university or national lab on product development.
You prefer a royalty over giving up equity.
skipIf: You only have an idea and no data (try BIG or E-YUVA first).
Your project needs clinical or multi-location field trials (BIPP fits better).
You cannot fund any share of the project or accept a sales royalty.
insiderTips: Check BIRAC's Call for Proposals page often; SBIRI and BIPP calls have usually opened together on 1 April or mid-September.
If you are a startup under 10 years old with no previous BIRAC grant, design the first ₹50 lakh of your budget carefully, because that part can be fully funded.
Bring hard preliminary data; the guidelines say proposals without it 'will NOT be supported'.

performance.summary: Since 2005, SBIRI had announced 53 calls and supported 337 projects with ₹576 crore committed as of 31 January 2024, according to BIRAC's scheme page. BIRAC does not publish year-wise figures for SBIRI.

name: Biotechnology Industry Partnership Programme (BIPP)
provider: BIRAC, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Grant-in-aid on a cost-sharing basis with no fixed cap ('costs commensurate with activities'). A startup with no earlier BIRAC grant gets up to 100% of its budget up to ₹50 lakh plus up to 70% above that; other companies get up to 70%. 5% royalty on product sales until it equals the grant.
equity: None, but 5% royalty on annual net sales until total royalty equals the grant
timeToMoney: Not published. Expert review and committee approval, then grant and royalty agreements before the first instalment.
deadline: Last call ran 1 Apr – 30 May 2025. Guidelines describe two calls a year, but none was listed on BIRAC's call page after May 2025 as of 27 Oct 2026.
oneLiner: BIRAC's big-ticket grant for breakthrough, late-stage biotech development, including clinical and field trials.
what: BIPP funds high-risk, transformational biotech product and process development that should end at TRL 7 or above. It covers four categories: (I/II) socially important or globally competitive innovation research, (III-A) Phase III clinical trials, (III-B) multi-location agriculture field trials, and (IV) shared facilities critical for innovation. It is grant-in-aid with industry co-funding and IP owned by the Indian company.
who: A company (Companies Act 2013) or LLP, alone or with public/private research partners.
At least 51% of shares held by Indian citizens with Indian passports; for LLPs at least half the partners must be Indian citizens.
Adequate in-house facilities (checked on site) or incubation at a recognised incubator.
A project with transformational, not incremental, technology that can reach TRL 7 or higher.
notFor: Incremental improvements to existing products.
Companies (or directors) in default on BIRAC loans, refunds or royalties.
Early-idea projects without proof of concept (use BIG or SBIRI).
why: No published cap: suited to expensive late-stage work such as clinical or multi-location field trials.
Grant money with IP retained by your company.
Signals to investors and partners that your technology passed a tough national review.
246 projects supported and 95 products/technologies developed or commercialised as of 31 Jan 2024.
howItWorks: BIRAC invites proposals through calls on its portal; it may also run special or challenge calls on specific national needs. Expert panels evaluate novelty, preliminary data, strength of proof of concept, strategy, national relevance, team credentials and commercial potential. Approved projects sign a grant agreement and a royalty agreement. Funds are released in instalments linked to technical milestones. The company co-funds as per the cost-sharing rules and pays a 5% royalty on net sales until it equals the grant.

steps.title: Confirm category and TRL
steps.detail: Pick the right BIPP category (I/II, III-A clinical, III-B field trials, IV facilities) and show the project can end at TRL 7+.

steps.title: Register on the BIRAC portal
steps.detail: Register your company on birac.nic.in and read the BIPP user guide and category proforma.

steps.title: Prepare co-funding and partners
steps.detail: Plan your share of costs and any academic or clinical partners.

steps.title: Submit during an active call
steps.detail: File online with milestones, budget, regulatory plan and commercialisation path.

steps.title: Expert evaluation and site visit
steps.detail: Respond to reviewer questions; BIRAC checks facilities.

steps.title: Sign agreements and start
steps.detail: Sign the Grant-in-aid Letter Agreement and royalty agreement, complete board resolution and no-lien account formalities, then receive the first instalment.

pros: No published funding ceiling.
Covers clinical and field trials, which few grants do.
No equity dilution.
Clear cost-sharing rules.
cons: Co-funding required beyond a startup's first ₹50 lakh (at least 30%).
5% royalty on sales until it equals the grant.
No call listed since May 2025.
Best suited to companies with strong teams, data and regulatory know-how; tough for first-time founders.
goodFitIf: You have a validated biotech product heading into trials or scale-up.
You can co-fund part of a large project.
Your innovation is breakthrough rather than incremental.
skipIf: You are at idea or early proof-of-concept stage.
You cannot co-fund or accept a sales royalty.
Your project is an incremental improvement.
insiderTips: Use BIRAC's published evaluation parameters per category (linked on the BIPP page) as your outline.
BIPP and SBIRI calls have opened on the same dates; prepare both options and choose based on your TRL.
For Category III projects, get your regulatory pathway (CDSCO or GEAC) mapped before applying.

name: BIRAC SEED Fund and LEAP Fund (equity support via BioNEST incubators)
provider: BIRAC, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: SEED Fund: up to ₹30 lakh per startup as equity or equity-linked investment. LEAP Fund: up to ₹1 crore per startup, in one or more milestone tranches. Both are invested by BIRAC-approved BioNEST incubators.
equity: Equity or equity-linked instruments (e.g. CCDs/CCPS) held by the incubator; terms set by each incubator
duration: One-time investment; LEAP can be released in milestone tranches
timeToMoney: Not published; depends on each partner incubator's own selection and investment process.
deadline: No national deadline. Each SEED/LEAP partner incubator runs its own intake (open calls, accelerators or direct applications).
oneLiner: BIRAC money invested as equity through top bio-incubators: up to ₹30 lakh (SEED) after proof of concept, and up to ₹1 crore (LEAP) to pilot or launch.
what: SEED (Sustainable Entrepreneurship and Enterprise Development) is aimed at post-proof-of-concept biotech startups and is meant to bridge the gap between founders' own money and angel investment. LEAP (Launching Entrepreneurial Driven Affordable Products) supports startups going from proof of concept to pilot or commercial launch so they can raise venture capital. BIRAC gives the partner incubators a pool (up to ₹2 crore per cycle for SEED, up to ₹5 crore for LEAP), and the incubators choose startups and invest.
who: A startup company registered under the Companies Act 2013 with at least 51% Indian-citizen shareholders (OCI/PIO excluded).
Selected by one of BIRAC's SEED Fund partners (16 BioNEST incubators) or LEAP Fund partners (6 incubators).
SEED: post-proof-of-concept startups. LEAP: startups ready to pilot or commercialise and needing more than ₹30 lakh.
notFor: Startups that have already had SEED support (SEED is once per startup).
LEAP for startups whose SEED funding period has not finished, or was foreclosed or terminated.
Startups needing only up to ₹30 lakh (these go to SEED, not LEAP).
Concurrent SEED and LEAP support.
why: Fills the 'valley of death' between grants and VC money.
Comes with an experienced bio-incubator on your cap table.
BIRAC-reported outcomes: SEED startups raised ₹398 crore follow-on (71 startups) and LEAP startups ₹339 crore (27 startups) as of Feb 2023.
howItWorks: BIRAC selects established BioNEST incubators as partners and parks a grant-in-aid pool with each (up to ₹200 lakh per cycle for SEED, ₹500 lakh for LEAP). Each incubator designs its own selection (accelerator cohorts or direct investment) and an investment committee picks startups. The incubator invests as equity or equity-linked instruments and holds them in its own name. On exit, the incubator keeps 50% of the gross return and returns 50% to BIRAC. No management fee is charged to the startup by BIRAC.

steps.title: Find a partner incubator
steps.detail: Open the SEED or LEAP page on birac.nic.in and see the list of partner incubators (e.g. C-CAMP, IKP, SINE IIT Bombay, KIIT-TBI, FITT IIT Delhi, Venture Center).

steps.title: Get incubated or apply to their programme
steps.detail: Most partners invest in their own incubatees or accelerator cohorts; apply through the incubator's website.

steps.title: Prepare an investment pitch
steps.detail: Show proof of concept (SEED) or pilot/commercial readiness (LEAP), use of funds, milestones and cap table.

steps.title: Incubator investment committee review
steps.detail: Pitch to the incubator's committee; expect due diligence on IP, team and finances.

steps.title: Sign the investment agreement
steps.detail: Agree valuation and instrument (equity or convertible) with the incubator.

steps.title: Receive funds and report
steps.detail: LEAP may be released in tranches against milestones; you report progress to the incubator, which reports to BIRAC.

Pitch deck and business plan
Proof-of-concept or pilot data
IP status (patents filed or licences)
Financial statements and projections

benefits: Equity capital up to ₹30 lakh (SEED) or ₹1 crore (LEAP)
Incubator mentoring, lab access and investor networks
Signalling value for angel and VC rounds
pros: Rare institutional equity for biotech at pre-angel stage.
Startup-friendly investors who understand long biotech timelines.
Can be combined with grants such as BIG (sequentially).
cons: You give up equity, unlike BIRAC grants.
Access depends on getting into one of a few partner incubators.
Terms and timelines vary by incubator.
Published impact numbers are old (last updated Feb 2023).
goodFitIf: You have proof of concept (SEED) or a product ready to pilot (LEAP).
You are or can become incubated at a BIRAC SEED/LEAP partner.
You are comfortable giving equity for capital plus support.
skipIf: You only need grant money and want zero dilution.
You are at idea stage with no proof of concept.
You already received SEED (for SEED) or your SEED term is still running (for LEAP).
insiderTips: Treat incubator selection as a fundraising decision; partners differ a lot in follow-on success (BIRAC's LEAP table shows follow-on raised by each partner).
Line up a BIG grant first: grant-funded proof of concept makes the SEED conversation easier.
Ask the incubator up front about instrument, valuation method and timeline.

LEAP had 6 partners and 47 startups, which raised ₹339 crore follow-on (27 startups). Year-wise figures are not published.

name: E-YUVA: BIRAC E-YUVA Fellowship and BIRAC Innovation Fellowship
provider: BIRAC, Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Undergraduate teams (E-YUVA Fellows): ₹7,500 per student per quarter plus a ₹2.5 lakh research grant per team, for 12 months. Postgraduates/PhDs (Innovation Fellows): ₹30,000/month (master's) or ₹50,000/month (PhD) plus ₹3 lakh or ₹5 lakh per year research grant, for 18 months (extendable by 6).
equity: None. IP stays with the innovators.
duration: 12 months (UG teams); 18 months, extendable by 6 (Innovation Fellows)
timeToMoney: Not published. Applications are screened by the E-YUVA Centre, reviewed, and shortlisted applicants present to a technical expert committee; stipends start after the fellowship agreement.
deadline: Current call for E-YUVA Fellows and Innovation Fellows closes 31 Oct 2026, 5:30 PM.
oneLiner: BIRAC pays college students and fresh postgraduates to work on a biotech product idea at a university innovation centre, with mentoring and lab access.
what: E-YUVA (Empowering Youth for Undertaking Value Added Innovative Translational Research) builds an innovation habit among students. It runs through E-YUVA Centres at universities, each mentored by a BIRAC BioNEST bio-incubator. Undergraduate teams get a small stipend and a research grant to build a biotech product idea; recent master's and PhD graduates get a full-time monthly fellowship and research grant to work toward a startup.
who: E-YUVA Fellows: a team of up to 5 Indian students pursuing an undergraduate degree in any discipline (mixed disciplines encouraged), with a faculty mentor, applying through their college E-Cell, Institution's Innovation Council or incubation centre.
Innovation Fellows: an Indian who has completed a master's (apply within 3 years) or PhD (apply within 2 years) in any discipline; women are exempt from these time limits.
Innovation Fellows must work full-time at the E-YUVA Centre.
Proposals must aim at a biotech product or technology with societal or commercial potential.
notFor: School students (this is for undergraduates and above).
Students currently doing a PhD (cannot take the Innovation Fellowship) and fellows who want to start a PhD during the fellowship.
Pure basic research with no product angle.
OCI/PIO cardholders (only Indian citizens are eligible).
why: One of very few central schemes that put money directly in undergraduates' hands for an innovation project.
Access to a pre-incubation lab (3,000 sq ft or more) and the partner bio-incubator's advanced facilities.
Mentoring on IP, regulation and business from BIRAC's incubator network.
IP stays with you, which matters if you later start a company and apply for BIG.
howItWorks: BIRAC funds E-YUVA Centres (19 listed in July 2026) at universities and links each to a BioNEST bio-incubator as knowledge partner. Applications are invited nationally on the BIRAC portal; you list up to 3 preferred centres. Each centre checks eligibility, sends proposals to reviewers, and shortlists applicants to present before a technical expert committee that includes a BIRAC nominee. Selected fellows sign an agreement with the centre. UG stipends go quarterly to students' accounts after mentor approval; the UG research grant goes to the institute in two instalments (75% then 25%) and is managed by the mentor. UG fellows must spend 3–4 weeks at the centre or knowledge partner during the year.

name: Grand Challenges India (GCI)
provider: BIRAC and Department of Biotechnology (DBT), with the Gates Foundation and other partners
amountText: Varies by call. The May–July 2026 call on screening and diagnosis offered up to ₹50 lakh (exploratory, up to 12 months) or up to ₹2 crore (solution/product, up to 18 months). The 2023–24 climate-and-health call offered up to ₹80 lakh over 36 months.
timeToMoney: Not published; depends on each call's review timeline.
deadline: No GCI funding call open as of 27 Oct 2026. The latest (screening and diagnosis) closed 15 Jul 2026; watch BIRAC's Call for Proposals page.
oneLiner: Themed challenge grants from DBT, BIRAC and the Gates Foundation for Indian teams solving big health, sanitation and agriculture problems.
what: Grand Challenges India is a programme management unit at BIRAC, set up by DBT and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, that issues themed calls for scientific and technical solutions to big public-health and development problems. Calls have covered maternal and child health, infectious diseases, sanitation, agriculture and nutrition, climate change and health, and cost-disruptive diagnostics. Each call sets its own amounts, duration and eligible applicants.
who: Indian applicants working in India: academic and research institutions, public and private R&D organisations, startups and not-for-profit foundations (2026 diagnostics call).
Earlier calls also listed Indian companies, trusts and medical research institutions; check each call's 'Who can apply'.
Global partners can join some calls, but most of the funding must go to investigators in India (for example at least 80% in the climate-and-agriculture call).
notFor: Proposals where most of the work will not be done by investigators living in India.
Projects without a pathway to sustainable impact and scale.
Applications sent outside the BIRAC online portal.
why: Large grants (up to ₹2 crore in the 2026 call) with no equity.
Global health network and visibility through Gates Foundation and partner programmes.
Startups are explicitly eligible in recent calls.
howItWorks: GCI publishes a request for proposals (RFP) per theme on BIRAC's portal, usually open for about two months. Proposals are reviewed by experts against the call's criteria; successful teams sign agreements and receive milestone-based funding. Calls are irregular and theme-driven rather than on a fixed calendar.

name: NIDHI-PRAYAS 2.0 (Promoting and Accelerating Young and Aspiring Innovators and Startups)
provider: Department of Science & Technology (DST), Ministry of Science & Technology; PMU: SINE, IIT Bombay
amountText: Prototype grant of up to ₹20 lakh at a PRAYAS Centre, or up to ₹40 lakh at an Advance PRAYAS Centre for deep-tech (PRAYAS 2.0 guidelines, March 2026). Up to 20% of the grant can be a sustenance allowance if you have no other income.
duration: 15 months per project, extendable by up to 6 months
timeToMoney: Not published; each PRAYAS Centre runs its own call, screening and committee decision before the first tranche.
deadline: No national deadline. Each PRAYAS Centre (host incubator) announces its own calls; check the NIDHI-PRAYAS website and centre websites.
oneLiner: A DST grant of up to ₹20–40 lakh for individuals or very young startups to build a physical prototype at a maker-lab incubator.
what: NIDHI-PRAYAS pays innovators to turn an idea into a working physical prototype. It is run through PRAYAS Centres at DST-supported incubators, each with a 'DST NIDHI Maker Bhavan' fabrication lab (3D printers, CNC, PCB tools and so on). The grant covers raw materials, fabrication, outsourced design or testing, patent filing (up to 10%) and limited travel. Version 2.0 (2026) raised the ceiling from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh, and to ₹40 lakh at Advance PRAYAS Centres for deep-tech.
who: An individual innovator (no company needed) or an early-stage startup.
Individuals and startup co-founders must be Indian citizens aged 18 or above on the application date.
Startups: incorporated in India for not more than 5 years, at least 51% Indian-held, annual turnover never above ₹1 crore.
The prototype must be a tangible physical product based on science or technology, buildable within 15 months.
Full-time students or employees must submit an NOC from their institution/employer allowing the project and confirming IP will belong to the innovator.
notFor: Pure software, e-commerce, service or app-based projects.
Products already past MVP stage.
Anyone under 18 (so most school students are not eligible).
Applicants who have received more than ₹40 lakh in total government grants, or who take parallel NIDHI-EIR support for the same idea.
Funding academic research or student internships.
why: No company and no equity needed: an individual can get the grant.
Access to a fully equipped fabrication lab plus mentors at the centre.
Up to ₹40 lakh for deep-tech prototypes is large for this stage.
Women and young innovators get preference.
howItWorks: DST funds PRAYAS Centres (PCs) and Advance PRAYAS Centres (APCs) at host incubators, giving each up to ₹2 crore (PC) or ₹4 crore (APC) a year for prototype grants plus money for a fab lab and operations. Each centre is expected to support around ten innovators a year. Innovators apply to a centre; a PRAYAS Local Monitoring Committee selects 'PRAYASEEs' and fixes the grant amount. Funds go to the lead innovator's account in tranches; the prototype must be ready within 15 months of the first tranche. SINE, IIT Bombay acts as the national programme management unit.

No equity or repayment.

You already have an MVP and customers.
You are under 18.

If you already got PRAYAS 1.0 money, you can only apply again at an Advance PRAYAS Centre for the balance up to ₹40 lakh.
Budget smartly: travel, patent filing and contingency are each capped at 10% of the approved cost.

name: NIDHI Entrepreneur-in-Residence (NIDHI-EIR)
provider: Department of Science & Technology (DST), Ministry of Science & Technology; PMU: Venture Center, Pune
amountText: Monthly fellowship of ₹10,000 to ₹30,000 for up to 12 months (maximum ₹3.6 lakh), plus incubator space and mentoring.
timeToMoney: Not published; depends on the EIR centre's selection cycle.
deadline: No national deadline. NIDHI-EIR centres (selected incubators/TBIs) run their own calls.
oneLiner: A DST fellowship that pays fresh graduates up to ₹30,000 a month for a year to work full-time on their startup idea inside an incubator.
what: NIDHI-EIR gives a living stipend to graduates who want to become entrepreneurs instead of taking a job, so they can explore a technology business idea with less personal risk. It is sector-agnostic. Fellows sit at a NIDHI-EIR centre (a DST-supported incubator), use its infrastructure and get mentoring, technical and financial advice and industry connections.
who: Indian citizens who are graduating or recently graduated students (DST describes it as a fellowship for graduate students).

Example centre rule (Venture Center, Pune): undergraduate training in science, engineering or medicine; a degree such as BTech, MSc, MBBS, MBA or PhD; BSc holders need 1 year of work or research experience.
Can apply as an individual or with a very new company (Venture Center: incorporated less than 1 year).
Must commit full-time and register with the centre's incubation programme for the fellowship period.
notFor: People holding another job, salary or fellowship at the same time.
Those using it as a stop-gap during academic studies.
Ideas with little or no technology innovation, or with a very short path to market.
Anyone also taking NIDHI-PRAYAS support for the same idea.
why: Pays your living costs while you test a startup idea.
Puts you inside an incubator with mentors and investor access from day one.
Good bridge from campus to founder for final-year students and fresh graduates.
howItWorks: DST selects incubators as NIDHI-EIR centres. Each centre advertises calls, screens applicants and has a committee choose fellows. The centre pays the fellowship monthly (between ₹10,000 and ₹30,000) for up to 12 months, and fellows report progress and work on business plans, prototypes and fundraising. Venture Center, Pune serves as DST's programme partner.

No equity.

goodFitIf: You are graduating or just graduated and want to work full-time on a tech startup idea.

name: NIDHI Seed Support Program (NIDHI-SSP, earlier NIDHI-SSS)
provider: Department of Science & Technology (DST), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Up to ₹1 crore per startup, invested by a DST-supported incubator (each incubator can get up to ₹10 crore from DST). Many incubators cap typical support at ₹25 lakh and go higher only in exceptional cases.
equity: Depends on the incubator: soft loan, equity or equity-linked instrument
duration: One-time seed support; loans typically repaid within 5 years (incubator terms)
timeToMoney: Not published; set by each incubator's seed committee.
deadline: No national deadline; incubators announce periodic calls for their incubatees.
oneLiner: DST money that incubators invest in their startups, up to ₹1 crore, for prototypes, trials and market entry.
what: NIDHI-SSP gives incubators a seed fund so they can quickly back promising startups they incubate. The money can pay for proof of concept, prototype development, product trials, market entry and commercialisation. Startups do not apply to DST directly; they apply to a listed incubator, which decides the amount and instrument.
who: Startups incubated at an incubator supported under NIDHI-SSP (list on DST's NIDHI-SSP page).
Typical incubator rules (e.g. FITT IIT Delhi): a registered Indian company, at least 3 months' residency at the incubator, at least 51% held by Indian promoters.
Innovators can also approach listed incubators, which then incubate them.
notFor: Startups not incubated at a NIDHI-SSP incubator.
Indian subsidiaries of foreign companies (as per incubator rules).
Startups that already received seed support at another TBI under the scheme (one-time support).
why: Bigger cheques (up to ₹1 crore) than most incubator seed funds.
Decisions are made locally by your incubator, which knows you.
Can be structured as a loan, so you may avoid dilution.
howItWorks: DST gives selected incubators up to ₹10 crore, released in phases. The incubator runs calls, screens startups, and a seed support committee decides who gets money and in what form (loan, equity or equity-linked). Returns and repayments go back into the incubator's seed pool for future startups.

name: Technology Development Board (TDB) Financial Assistance
provider: Technology Development Board, Department of Science & Technology (DST), Ministry of Science & Technology
amountText: Soft loan at 5% simple interest for up to 50% of the not-yet-spent project cost; equity up to 25% of approved project cost; grants only in exceptional cases. The 2025 startup call funded up to 70% of projects up to ₹5 crore (max ₹3.5 crore), and 50% above that.

timeToMoney: Not published. Applications go through technical and financial evaluation and Board approval; money is released in tranches against milestones.
deadline: Core funding applications accepted online year-round. Themed calls (e.g. startups, medical technologies) have their own deadlines; the 2025 startup call closed 10 Apr 2025.
oneLiner: A government lender that funds Indian companies to commercialise home-grown technology, mainly through cheap 5% loans.
what: TDB was set up in 1996 to fund the commercial use of indigenous technology or the adaptation of imported technology. It lends to companies at 5% simple interest, can take equity, and occasionally gives grants. It suits companies that have proven their technology and now need capital to scale manufacturing or launch, rather than early research.
who: Indian companies (industrial concerns) incorporated under the Companies Act commercialising indigenous technology.
For the 2025 startup call: DPIIT-recognised startups at Technology Readiness Level above 6.

notFor: Idea-stage or pure research projects (TDB funds commercialisation).
Individuals without a company.

why: Cheap capital: 5% simple interest with a one-year moratorium after project completion.

Large ticket sizes for manufacturing scale-up.

TDB normally lends up to 50% of the unspent project cost; you bring the rest. Money is disbursed in tranches tied to technical and financial milestones. After completion there is a one-year moratorium, then repayment in instalments. TDB also co-runs international bilateral calls (Israel, UK, Sweden, Singapore and others) that give conditional grants.

what: Under Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY), the Agriculture Ministry funds agri-startups through Knowledge Partners (such as IARI Pusa, NIAM Jaipur, MANAGE Hyderabad, UAS Dharwad, AAU Jorhat, IIT Kanpur, IRRI Varanasi) and RKVY Agribusiness Incubators (R-ABIs) at agricultural universities and institutes. name: Pradhan Mantri Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PMFME) Scheme
provider: Ministry of Food Processing Industries (MoFPI), with State nodal agencies
amountText: Individual units: 35% credit-linked capital subsidy on project cost, up to ₹10 lakh per unit (you put in at least 10%, a bank loan covers the rest). SHG members: seed capital of ₹40,000 each. Groups/FPOs: 35% grant with credit linkage; support for common infrastructure and branding.

oneLiner: A 35% subsidy (up to ₹10 lakh) on a bank loan to start or upgrade a small food-processing unit, plus help with training, FSSAI and branding.
what: PMFME helps micro food-processing businesses (pickles, spices, bakery, dairy, millets, snacks and so on) upgrade machinery, get formal registrations and grow. It gives a credit-linked capital subsidy, seed capital to Self Help Group members, grants for common facilities and incubation centres, branding and marketing support, and training. It follows a One District One Product (ODOP) approach that prioritises each district's signature product.
who: Individual micro food-processing enterprises, existing or new, that take a bank loan for the project.

The application is checked by the district and State nodal agency and forwarded to a bank. Once the bank sanctions the loan, the 35% subsidy (max ₹10 lakh) is released to the loan account. SHG seed capital is routed through SHG federations as a repayable loan to members.

name: Smart India Hackathon (SIH)
provider: Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell (MIC) with AICTE
amountText: ₹1,00,000 prize per problem statement for the winning team (software and hardware editions), per SIH's official FAQ. Some 2025 nodal centres reported ₹1.5 lakh; check the current edition's rules.
equity: None. IP of a winning solution may be shared with the organisation that posed the problem.

timeToMoney: Prize after the Grand Finale (typically held in December), only if the problem-statement owner accepts the winning solution.
deadline: SIH 2026 team nomination and idea submission closed 9 Oct 2026 (extended). The next edition's problem statements are usually released mid-year.
oneLiner: India's national student hackathon: college teams of six solve real government and industry problems and win ₹1 lakh per problem statement.
what: SIH gives higher-education students real problem statements from central ministries, state governments, PSUs and industry. Colleges run internal hackathons and nominate their best teams; shortlisted teams build working solutions at a Grand Finale held at nodal centres across India. Winners get prize money and some solutions are taken up by ministries, with alumni going on to found startups.
who: Students of higher-education institutions (SIH Senior) in teams of 6 students (plus up to 2 mentors), including at least one female member.

notFor: Teams not nominated through their institution's internal hackathon.

howItWorks: Ministries, departments, PSUs and companies submit problem statements; MIC publishes them. Each college's SPOC registers, runs an internal hackathon and nominates its best teams. Team leaders submit ideas on the portal; around 6 students and 2 mentors make up each nominated team. Problem-statement owners evaluate and shortlist teams for the Grand Finale, held simultaneously at nodal centres (60 in 2025). One winning team per problem statement receives the prize, if the owner accepts the solution.

name: INSPIRE-MANAK (Million Minds Augmenting National Aspirations and Knowledge)
provider: Department of Science & Technology (DST) with National Innovation Foundation – India (NIF)
amountText: ₹10,000 by direct bank transfer to each of up to 1 lakh selected students to build a model or prototype of their idea; top ideas go on to district, state and national competitions, mentoring and patent support.
duration: Annual cycle: nominations (around June–October), award money, then district, state and national exhibitions
timeToMoney: Not published; award money is paid by DBT after shortlisting, months after nominations close.
deadline: Nominations for 2026-27 closed (deadline extended to 10 Oct 2026). The next round usually opens mid-year; schools nominate on the portal.
sectors: Any (science and technology ideas from school students)
oneLiner: DST's national idea competition for Class 6–12 students: your school nominates your idea and, if selected, you get ₹10,000 to build it.
what: INSPIRE-MANAK, run by DST and NIF, aims to collect one million original ideas from school students and turn the best into prototypes. Each school can nominate its five best student ideas a year (up to two from Class 11–12 science). Selected students receive ₹10,000 to build a model and take part in a District Level Exhibition; about 10% move to State level, and up to around 1,000 to the National Level Exhibition and Project Competition, where the top 60 are recognised and supported by NIF.
who: Students of Classes 6 to 12 in any recognised school (government, aided or private) in India.
Nominated by the school (Principal/Headmaster) after an internal idea competition.
Each school can nominate up to 5 ideas a year, of which at most 2 can be from Classes 11–12 (science stream only).
Ideas can be submitted in any Indian language.
notFor: Students who apply on their own without school nomination.
College students (see Smart India Hackathon, E-YUVA or NIDHI-PRAYAS).
Class 11–12 students from non-science streams (per the portal rules).
Copied or non-original ideas.
why: Real money (₹10,000) in a school student's own bank account to build their idea.
National exposure: winners have met the President at FINE and visited Japan under the Sakura Science programme.
NIF files patents for promising ideas (255 filed, 34 granted, 2017–2024).
Bonus admission points at some institutions (e.g. IIIT Delhi gives 2 points to NLEPC award winners).
howItWorks: Schools register on the INSPIRE-MANAK portal and nominate students' idea synopses. NIF and DST shortlist about 1 lakh ideas; those students get ₹10,000 by direct benefit transfer to make a prototype and exhibit at the District Level Exhibition and Project Competition (DLEPC). About 10% go to State level (SLEPC), and selected students go to the National Level Exhibition (NLEPC), where the top 60 get further mentoring, IP filing and product development support from NIF, often in partnership with IITs and NITs.

performance.summary: Since its 2016 revamp, INSPIRE-MANAK nominations grew from just over 1.56 lakh in FY 2016-17 to over 11.47 lakh in FY 2025-26, totalling 61,10,183 ideas in ten years from 99% of districts. 3,91,777 students received ₹10,000 prototype grants over that period, and 49,805 students were supported in 2025-26. NIF filed 255 patents for students between 2017 and 2024 (34 granted).

name: Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL)
amountText: Grant to the school of up to ₹20 lakh over 5 years: up to ₹10 lakh one-time for equipment (3D printer, electronics, DIY kits) in year one, plus ₹10 lakh over up to 5 years for running costs, consumables and events.
duration: Up to 5 years of grant-in-aid to the school
timeToMoney: Not published; schools are shortlisted from applications and funds are released in tranches after compliance.
deadline: Applications open in rounds. In 2026 AIM invited schools in frontier regions (e.g. Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, North-East, aspirational districts) under AIM 2.0; separately, 50,000 ATLs in government schools are being rolled out for 2025-26.
oneLiner: AIM gives schools up to ₹20 lakh to build a maker lab where Class 6–12 students tinker with 3D printers, robotics and electronics.
what: Atal Tinkering Labs are makerspaces in schools that let students learn design thinking, coding, electronics and prototyping by building things. The grant goes to the school, not to students, but students get free access to equipment and to programmes such as the ATL Marathon, the ATL Student Innovator Programme and mentoring by 'Mentors of Change'.
who: Schools (at least Classes 6–10) run by Central/State Government, local bodies, private trusts/societies or tribal/social welfare departments.
Schools need about 750 sq ft of all-weather space, a computer lab with internet and steady electricity (frontier-region guidelines).
Students of Classes 6–12 use the lab once their school has one.
notFor: Individual students (they cannot apply directly).
Schools that cannot meet the space, internet and staffing criteria.
Using the grant for anything other than the ATL (unspent money must be refunded).
why: Gives students hands-on access to tools usually found only in colleges.
Feeds into national challenges like the ATL Marathon and ATL Student Innovator Programme.
Builds a portfolio for INSPIRE-MANAK, science fairs and later SIH.
howItWorks: AIM invites schools to apply online. Applications are screened on infrastructure, faculty and reach; selected schools sign terms, set up an advisory body (including parents) and receive the establishment grant in the first year, followed by operational grants over up to 5 years, against annual utilisation certificates and activity reports.
